questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to live in a city where french was the main language spoken, and also a bigger city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was alright. ULB has a website that is good for orientation, however, it works best in French.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received a welcome pdf from ULB and then we had an introduction seminar the week before classes started.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It was a bit hard to figure out what the schedule for the courses was a long time in advance, but it was available the week before classes started.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was not that difficult to find off-campus housing. I found it via the Facebook group "Danskere i Belgien", but my impression is that many people find it through their network/facebook groups. There are also houses called "Dansker-huse" which is owned by a woman called Helene.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It was great living off campus since it made it possible to see other parts of the city than the one ULB is in. Also, ULB does not allow exchange students to stay in any of their dorms. I can recommend the areas Saint-Gilles, Ixelles, Etterbeck, and Saint-Josse. Some parts of town are quite sketchy, especially around the stations Gare du Nord and Gare du Midi.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: No need to worry about the cost of public transportation if you find a place far from the university, since it's only 12€ for a whole year (!) of public transportation for students under 25.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system of course registration is quite different from the one in Copenhagen as the first three weeks of courses just is "shopping weeks" where you can try out the different courses you like, and then just have to confirm what courses you are taking once those weeks have passed.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course registration happens through a Word document, which is sent to the academic coordinator three weeks after the semester begins. Written exams are registered for automatically.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is an online website (TE viewer) available a week before the semester starts where it is possible to see if there are any conflicts in the schedule.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted in the end. However, some of the ones I originally wanted had overlapping schedules.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't stress about the course registration, and that it isn't available until a week before the semester starts. The academic coordinator at ULB is super nice, and wants help solve any issue you have with the courses/schedules. Note that bachelor's students are only allowed to take two masters courses per semester. However, the academic coordinator game me permission to take three due to challenges with my schedule.

It is possible to get by without being fluent in French at ULB. Although, many bachelor's programs are only in French, but many masters are in English.

The university buildings in itself are not that pretty, but the overall teaching is at a good level.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The teachers were nice. Some did have accents though (French, Italian, German).

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I took three master's courses and three bachelor's courses, even though bachelor exchange students normally are only allowed to take two master's courses. However, after emailing back and forth with the academic coordinator at ULB, I got permission. 

The overall level was similar to what I'm used to at UCPH. Exams are often closed book, handwritten and multiple-choice. I found that exams for the bachelor's courses were harder to pass than the ones at the master's courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For my bachelor's courses, I had lectures and for my master's courses, I had smaller seminars (like holdtimer), which is also what I'm used to at UCPH. In general, there was less student participation during class than what I'm used to, but for the master's courses it was a bit more participatory.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Introduction to Political Science (BA), Institutions and Political Representation (MA), Introduction to European Politics (BA), European Integration and Public Policy (MA), Gender and Social Movements (MA), Introduction to Political Communication (BA).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I liked the professor at Institutions and Political Representation (MA) a lot, and the class was often open for discussion. Also, the Gender and Social Movements (MA) class had a nice professor, and the topics covered were interesting as well was the readings.

Food DKK per month *

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Getting home in the night can require taking an Uber/Bolt, since the public transportation in Brussels often ends at 2am/3am, even in the weekends.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Public transport is only 12€ for students under 25, which is very cheap. Food pricing is approx. the same as in Copenhagen. Coffee and beer are cheaper :)) The Royal Library is not free to study at, but costs 15€ for a year subscription.

I didn't have to buy any books for my classes at ULB. 

Traveling with Flixbus to other big cities (Paris, Antwerp, Amsterdam) can be quite cheap if booked time in advance.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
ULB has a sports card for 36€ per semester, where a lot of different sports are included: Team sports (rugby, basketball), individual sports (badminton, fencing), music classes (zumba, salsa, Body Sculpt), and much more (cheerleading, tai chi, etc.). 

There are also some student associations called Cercles, but those are more for local students and have some interesting - and a bit outdated - traditions/activities.

For the exchange students, ULB has an Erasmus Student Network (ESN) that hosts a lot of activities throughout the semester like Bowling, museum visits, pub crawls, running clubs, parties and more (follow their Instagram @esnulbbrussels for more info).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The sports I can personally recommend are zumba, stretching, and salsa. 

The St V Day (November 20th) is really fun. Also, the CPS Cercle hosted a big barbeque party in the beginning of the semester, which was fun.

The ESN things are fun to attend as well and a good way to meet new people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Things to do in Brussels: 
- Museums: Magritte museum, Migrant museum, Africa museum
- Cafes: Le Pain Quotidien, Belga & Co., Living room
- Food: Yummy bowl, Maison Antoine (fries), Le botaniste
- Markets: Jeu de balle (all days), Flagey (only weekends)

Other places to go: Antwerp, Lille, Paris, Gent.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it quite easy. In general, everything starts later timewise; eating times, courses, etc.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to the containers behind the canteen in the evenings to get cheap beer and talk to local students. Also, go to Place de Luxembourg on Thursday afternoons/evenings to talk to locals and international workers in Brussels in general.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There is way less structure in Brussels in general compared to Copenhagen. This is in regard to being on time (both with friends and for classes), course registration, public transportation, etc.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The city is so diverse, which I found very refreshing. In general, it is easy being a foreigner in Brussels, as there are so many of them.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be open-minded and curious. Most people are going to be friendly, and the bus driver will always wait for you if you run <3

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Brussels can be a bit dangerous, and there are many homeless people at the metro stations and on the streets. As a woman, the city can feel a bit does feel a bit unsafe, especially at night. So I would always recommend being aware of one's surroundings when going home at night, texting friends when arriving at home, and taking an Uber if one is going home from a sketchy neighborhood.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many fun and interesting people from all over the world. I have learned so much about other cultures, both European and outside of Europe (especially Middle Eastern, African, and South American). Brussels, being the most culturally diverse city in Europe, is the perfect place to meet and connect with people from all over the world. Also, people are so nice if you don't speak perfect French since there are so many foreigners in the city.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The weather can be a bit depressing (it rains A LOT). Making friends abroad always takes some effort, but I didn't find it that hard in Brussels.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: The city might be a bit of a mess aesthetically, but being a cultural melting pot is what makes it interesting to live in.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
